subject: Climate & Environment
title: Southeast Asian Rainforests
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Southeast Asian Rainforests.

hook.text: Borneo's rainforest is 140 million years old — older than the Amazon by 80 million years.

buildup.text: Southeast Asia holds some of the highest biodiversity per square meter on the planet.

discovery.text: Orangutans, tigers, and rhinoceros all depend on these forests for survival.

twist.text: Palm oil plantations have replaced over 30% of Borneo's original forest since 1973.

climax.text: Southeast Asia has the highest deforestation rate of any tropical region.

punchline.text: The oldest rainforest on Earth is vanishing the fastest.

details.summary: Southeast Asian rainforests on Borneo, Sumatra, and the Malay Peninsula have the highest deforestation rate of any tropical region, driven primarily by palm oil, pulp, and rubber plantations. These forests host orangutans, tigers, and exceptionally high tree diversity.
details.whyItMatters: Southeast Asia has lost more than half its original forest cover. Its rapid deforestation provides a case study in how commodity demand drives tropical destruction.
takeaways: Borneo lost over 30 percent of its forest between 1973 and 2020
Palm oil expansion is the single largest deforestation driver
Peat forest destruction releases enormous stored carbon and methane

faq.question: Why is peatland deforestation especially damaging?
faq.answer: Tropical peatlands store centuries of accumulated carbon in waterlogged soil. When drained for plantations, the peat dries, decomposes, and catches fire, releasing massive CO2 and toxic haze that blankets the region for months.

faq.question: Has demand for sustainable palm oil slowed deforestation?
faq.answer: Certification schemes like RSPO have raised awareness, but certified palm oil accounts for only about 19 percent of global supply. Weak enforcement and continuing demand growth mean deforestation has slowed but not stopped.
